passage:
Dear Lalremsiami,
I've started this letter four times. Here is the true version.
On the class trip, at the dhaba, I laughed when Kunal read out your diary page, and I said, "Give it here, let's see more." When you brought it up last week, I told you it never happened. Then I said you were too sensitive and always twist things. I said it so firmly that you apologised to me. I watched you apologise for something I did.
I keep asking myself why. I think I couldn't stand being someone who laughs at a friend. I'm supposed to be the nice one. So I erased it instead of owning it, and made you carry the doubt.
It did happen. You remembered it exactly right. I'm sorry for the laugh, and sorrier for the lie after.
I'll be at the library bench after school on Friday, if you want to talk. If you don't, I understand.
Nirmala

qa.q: Where did Kunal read out the diary page?
qa.a: Kunal read out the diary page at the dhaba on the class trip.

qa.q: What feeling does Nirmala think led to the denial?
qa.a: Nirmala felt ashamed at being someone who laughs at a friend and wanted to stay the nice one, so erasing the event felt easier than owning it.

qa.q: Which line in the letter matters most, and why?
qa.a: "It did happen. You remembered it exactly right" matters most, because it gives Lalremsiami back trust in their own memory, which the apology alone would not do.

qa.q: What was it like for Lalremsiami to be told the event never happened?
qa.a: Lalremsiami was left doubting a clear memory and even apologised for being hurt, carrying a confusion that belonged to Nirmala.

grounding: A student writes to a friend admitting to denying a hurtful moment and calling the friend too sensitive, to protect a nice self-image, and now names the truth.

passage:
Tenzin, can I tell you something I'm not proud of? You know my little brother Arun's clay elephant, the one for the school exhibition? Last month I knocked it off the shelf while dancing. The trunk snapped. I glued it and put it back.
When he found the crack, I said, "It was always like that. You made it that way." He said no, he remembered it perfect. I said, "Arun, you always imagine things." I said it calmly, the way Amma does when she's sure.
Yesterday he asked me, really small, "Lakshmi Akka, do I remember things wrong a lot?" And I felt sick. He's nine. He believed me over his own eyes.
I did it on purpose. I just didn't want the scolding. So tonight I'm telling him, and Amma, what really happened, and saying sorry for the lie too. Will you text me after dinner, so I don't back out?

qa.q: What did Lakshmi knock off the shelf?
qa.a: Lakshmi knocked Arun's clay elephant off the shelf, and the trunk snapped.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel when Arun asked if he remembers things wrong?
qa.a: She felt sick with guilt, seeing that her little brother had started to doubt his own eyes because of her.

qa.q: What choice is Lakshmi making tonight, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She has decided to tell Arun and Amma what really happened, which gives Arun back trust in his memory and puts the blame where it belongs.

qa.q: What might it be like for Arun to hear the truth from his sister?
qa.a: He may feel upset about the elephant but also relieved and steadier, knowing his memory was right all along.

grounding: An older sister tells Tenzin she deliberately denied breaking her brother's clay elephant and said he imagines things, until he began doubting himself.

passage:
"You said my teeth look like a rabbit's. In front of everyone at the canteen." Neelam's voice was shaking.
Jatin laughed. "I never said that."
"You did. Yesterday. Rohan laughed."
"Neelam, you're making things up. Or you heard wrong. You're way too sensitive."
"I'm not making it up."
"See, this is why nobody jokes with you."
"So you did say it? As a joke?"
"I didn't say anything! God."
Their friend Kavya, sitting on the steps, looked up. "Jatin. I was there. You said it."
Jatin's face went red. He grabbed his bag. "Whatever. You're all against me."
He walked off fast. At home that evening, he kept replaying it. He wasn't the kind of guy who said mean things. Was he? It was easier to believe Neelam had misheard than to believe that.

qa.q: What did Neelam say Jatin compared her teeth to?
qa.a: A rabbit's.

qa.q: Why did Jatin keep insisting he never said it?
qa.a: Jatin felt ashamed and defensive, and could not bear to see himself as the kind of guy who says mean things.

qa.q: What could Jatin do to repair things?
qa.a: He could admit what he said, apologise to Neelam without calling her sensitive, and stop rewriting what happened.

qa.q: How did Neelam feel when Jatin said she was making things up?
qa.a: Neelam felt hurt and shaken, and doubted for a moment, until Kavya confirmed what happened.

grounding: It shows a teenager denying a hurtful remark and calling the other too sensitive to avoid blame, clinging to a self-image.

passage:
I'm Karthik, and last year I did something I'm still not proud of.
I shared an embarrassing photo of Binita in our class group. Her mouth full, eyes half shut. People sent laughing replies. Within an hour I deleted it.
The next day she asked me, "Why did you post that?" And I said, "What photo? I never posted anything. You're imagining it." When she showed me a screenshot, I said it must have been someone else using my phone. When she cried, I told her she was overreacting to nothing.
I think I knew. But I also couldn't stand being that guy. The mean one. So I kept saying it didn't happen until part of me almost believed it.
What stopped me was seeing her sit alone at lunch for a week. She looked like she didn't trust anything anymore, even her own eyes.
I finally told her the truth. And I told our class teacher too.

qa.q: What did Karthik say when Binita showed him a screenshot?
qa.a: Karthik said it must have been someone else using the phone.

qa.q: Why did Karthik keep denying he posted the photo?
qa.a: Karthik felt ashamed and couldn't stand seeing himself as the mean one, so he kept saying it didn't happen.

qa.q: What did Karthik finally do that was right?
qa.a: Karthik told Binita the truth and also told the class teacher.

qa.q: How did Binita feel during that week of denials?
qa.a: Binita felt hurt and confused, sitting alone and starting to doubt even her own eyes.

grounding: A teenager recalls denying sharing a photo and telling a classmate she was imagining it, to protect a self-image that could not bear the truth.

passage:
Class 9 teacher's note, Tuesday.
During the lunch line today, I saw Farhan push Payal hard with his shoulder. She stumbled into the railing and dropped her tray.
When I called them both over, Farhan said, "I didn't touch her. She tripped by herself. She's always making drama."
Payal's eyes filled. She said, quietly, "Maybe I tripped." I could see her doubting what had just happened to her.
I told them both, calmly, "I was standing right there. Farhan, you pushed her." Payal looked at me, surprised, and then her shoulders dropped with relief.
Farhan went red. He kept saying, "I'm not like that." Later, alone, he admitted he was angry about a joke she'd made in class, and pushing her felt like something "only bad kids do," so he couldn't say it.
I asked him to apologise to Payal and write down what he felt instead. I will speak to both families tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Payal drop when she stumbled?
qa.a: She dropped her tray.

qa.q: Why did Farhan deny pushing Payal?
qa.a: Farhan felt ashamed and angry, and couldn't admit something he saw as what "only bad kids do," so he blamed her instead.

qa.q: How did the teacher respond to Farhan's denial?
qa.a: The teacher calmly stated what they saw, asked Farhan to apologise and write about his feelings, and planned to speak to both families.

qa.q: How did Payal feel when the teacher confirmed what happened?
qa.a: Payal felt relieved, her shoulders dropping, after starting to doubt her own experience.

grounding: A teacher notes a teenager denying a push and calling the victim dramatic, clinging to a self-image that could not bear the truth.

passage:
Thursday night
Today Chetan said in front of everyone that on Monday in art period I called his drawing "baby scribbles". And I said, "I never said that. You're way too sensitive, seriously." Everyone laughed, and he went red and stared at his desk.
But I did say it. I remember exactly. I was annoyed because Ma'am praised his drawing and not mine.
Why did I lie so fast? I think because saying yes, I said it, felt like admitting I'm a mean person, and I'm not. I'm the one who always stands up for people. Or I thought I was.
The worst part was his face, like he was checking whether he'd made it all up.
Tomorrow before assembly I'll tell Chetan, just him: you didn't imagine it, I said it, I'm sorry. My hands are sweaty even writing that.
Nirmala

qa.q: What had Nirmala called Chetan's drawing on Monday?
qa.a: Nirmala called his drawing “baby scribbles” in art period.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala deny saying it?
qa.a: Nirmala felt ashamed and defensive; admitting it felt like admitting to being a mean person, which clashed with being the one who stands up for people.

qa.q: What makes Nirmala's plan for tomorrow a good repair?
qa.a: Telling Chetan privately that he didn't imagine it restores his trust in his own memory and owns the fault plainly.

qa.q: What was it like for Chetan to be told he was too sensitive?
qa.a: Chetan went red and stared at his desk, and seemed to wonder whether he had made it all up, so the denial hurt twice.

grounding: Shows a teenager denying a hurtful remark and calling the other too sensitive to avoid blame, driven by a self-image that could not bear the truth.
